```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7,
                      fig.height = 3.2, fig.align = "center", dpi = 96)
```

ProcEx evaluates classification models with more than two classes. It
answers four questions:

1. **Are the inputs usable?** Labels and predicted probabilities are checked
   before anything is computed.
2. **How well does the model separate the classes?** The Hand & Till (2001)
   multiclass AUC, with the AUC of every pair of classes.
3. **How sure can we be?** Bootstrap confidence intervals for one model, and
   a paired bootstrap comparison of two models.
4. **Where does the model struggle?** Plots of the pairwise ROC curves and
   AUCs show which pairs of classes are hard to tell apart.

ProcEx builds on the [pROC](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=pROC) package
and fills in the multiclass features pROC leaves out: confidence intervals,
model comparison and plots.

```{r setup}
library(ProcEx)
```

## Example data

We fit two multinomial models to the `iris` data: one uses the petal
measurements, the other only the sepal measurements. Each `predict()` call
returns one probability column per species, named after the species, which
is the form ProcEx expects.

```{r models}
petal_model <- nnet::multinom(Species ~ Petal.Length + Petal.Width,
                              data = iris, trace = FALSE)
sepal_model <- nnet::multinom(Species ~ Sepal.Length + Sepal.Width,
                              data = iris, trace = FALSE)

truth  <- iris$Species
petals <- predict(petal_model, type = "probs")
sepals <- predict(sepal_model, type = "probs")

round(sepals[c(1, 51, 101, 120), ], 3)   # one row per species, plus a hard one
```

(For a real evaluation, predict on data the model has not seen; the models
here are scored on their training data to keep the example short.)

## 1. Check the inputs

`validate_classification_data()` reports whether the labels and
probabilities can be analysed, and warns about things that make results less
reliable, such as very small or very unequal classes.

```{r validate}
checks <- validate_classification_data(truth, sepals)
checks$status
checks$class_counts
```

`mc_roc()` and `mc_auc_compare()` run these checks themselves, so you rarely
need to call it directly.

## 2. The multiclass AUC

`mc_roc()` computes the Hand & Till AUC. For every pair of classes it
measures how well the model ranks the two classes apart, and averages these
pairwise AUCs.

```{r mc-roc}
fit <- mc_roc(truth, sepals, label = "Sepal model")
fit
```

The overall AUC of `r round(fit$auc, 3)` looks good, but the pairwise table
shows it is an average of two perfect pairs and one much weaker pair:

```{r pairwise}
fit$pairwise
```

`auc_1v2` ranks the rows of the two classes by the probability of the first
class, `auc_2v1` by the probability of the second; the pair's AUC is their
mean.

## 3. Plot the pairwise curves

`plot()` draws each pair's two ROC curves, so a weak pair is visible at
once:

```{r plot-pairs, fig.height = 3}
plot(fit)
```

With many classes there are many pairs (7 classes give 21), so a heatmap is
easier to read. By default its colour scale stretches over the observed
AUCs, so the weakest pairs stand out:

```{r plot-heatmap, fig.width = 5, fig.height = 4}
plot(fit, type = "heatmap")
```

## 4. How sure can we be?

`mc_auc_ci()` resamples rows within each class (a stratified bootstrap) and
reports a percentile confidence interval for the AUC.

```{r ci}
ci <- mc_auc_ci(truth, sepals, n_boot = 200, seed = 1)
ci
```

The histogram shows the bootstrap AUCs; the shaded band is the confidence
interval and the solid line is the AUC of the original data.

```{r ci-plot, fig.height = 3.4}
plot(ci)
```

## 5. Compare two models

`mc_auc_compare()` asks whether the petal model is really better than the
sepal model, or whether the gap could be chance. Each bootstrap replicate
resamples the rows once and scores both models on those same rows, which
keeps the comparison paired. Model 1 is the petal model and Model 2 the
sepal model, in the order they are passed.

```{r compare}
comparison <- mc_auc_compare(truth, petals, sepals, n_boot = 500, seed = 1)
comparison
```

The interval for the difference does not include zero, so the petal model is
better at the 95% level. The plot shows the same thing: the shaded interval
lies to the right of the dashed zero line.

```{r compare-plot, fig.height = 3.6}
plot(comparison, labels = c("Petals", "Sepals"))
```

The per-pair AUCs show *where* the petal model gains: both models separate
*setosa* perfectly, so the whole difference comes from telling *versicolor*
from *virginica*.

```{r compare-pairwise}
comparison$pairwise
```

```{r compare-pairs, fig.height = 2.8}
plot(comparison, type = "pairs", labels = c("Petals", "Sepals"))
```

## 6. Missing values

`mc_roc()` keeps rows with a missing label or probability in the object but
leaves them out of the AUC, with a warning:

```{r missing}
with_gaps <- sepals
with_gaps[c(5, 70), "setosa"] <- NA
fit_gaps <- mc_roc(truth, with_gaps)
```

`mc_auc_ci()` stops when there are missing values, and `mc_auc_compare()`
passes them to pROC, so remove or fill missing values before running either.
For an `mc_roc` object, see `?handle_missing`.

## 7. Why the ROC direction is fixed

An ROC curve needs a direction: are higher scores expected for the first
class or the second? pROC's `roc()`, and `multiclass.roc()` with a single
score, default to `direction = "auto"`, which picks whichever direction
looks better *on the data being evaluated*. That choice favours the model,
so AUCs come out too high. On scores that are pure noise, where the true AUC
is 0.5:

```{r direction}
set.seed(1)
noise_auc <- replicate(200, {
  y <- factor(sample(c("a", "b"), 60, replace = TRUE))
  s <- runif(60)
  c(auto  = as.numeric(pROC::auc(pROC::roc(y, s, quiet = TRUE))),
    fixed = as.numeric(pROC::auc(pROC::roc(y, s, quiet = TRUE,
                                           direction = "<"))))
})
round(rowMeans(noise_auc), 3)
```

ProcEx always fixes the direction (the probability of a class should be
higher for rows of that class), so a model that is worse than chance gets an
AUC below 0.5 instead of being flipped to look good:

```{r worse-than-chance}
swapped <- sepals[, c("versicolor", "virginica", "setosa")]
colnames(swapped) <- colnames(sepals)    # probabilities given to the wrong class
mc_roc(truth, swapped)$auc
```

## Requirements and limits

* `mc_roc()`, `mc_auc_compare()` and the plots need at least three classes.
  `mc_auc_ci()` also handles two classes; for binary problems pROC itself
  offers more (DeLong intervals, `roc.test()`).
* Probabilities need one column per class, named exactly as the class labels
  (any order). `mc_roc()` also checks that values are between 0 and 1 and
  that rows sum to 1, and rejects scores that are not probabilities.
* Bootstrap intervals describe the uncertainty from which rows happened to
  be in the evaluation data; they do not include the variation from
  retraining the model.

See `NEWS.md` in the package source for changes and known issues.

## Reference

Hand, D. J. & Till, R. J. (2001). A simple generalisation of the area under
the ROC curve for multiple class classification problems. *Machine Learning*,
45, 171-186.
